questions: Does max_error drop below 0.06 m with the narrower, lighter, shorter robot, or does it still reach about 0.062 m?
Does the narrower track (0.09 m) make steering too twitchy, with higher steering_oscillation than the 0.12 m track?
Is progress higher than iteration 1 (oval about 0.31, s-bend about 0.15)? If not, is speed or the 0.6 kg mass now limiting?
Would a smaller sensor footprint (12 mm) at the same positions help the controller resolve the line more precisely?

intent: Make the robot more agile to close the tracking gap that left it off track at 0.062 m. The sensing array from iteration 1 is kept unchanged (it removed line loss). Narrower track, lighter mass and shorter body cut yaw inertia and raise the yaw response per steering command, so the controller can correct before the robot reaches the 0.06 m limit. Expected: max_error under 0.06 m on the oval and s-bend, line_loss_events near 0, and the first completions.
learning: Iteration 1 showed sensing is no longer the limit (line loss 0), but a 16 mm, 7-sensor array did not stop off-track failure and reduced progress. Body width is confirmed irrelevant to the 0.06 m limit. Next, test whether drivetrain agility (track, mass, body length) reduces max_error. If it does, keep the agility and tune further. If it does not, the remaining lever is the reaction point (sensor y) or the controller, and I will report that back.
rationale: Evidence from iteration 1: line loss fell from about 1 event per run to 0 across all three tracks, so the seven-sensor, 16 mm, 0.06 m-span array fixed sensing. Completions stayed at 0 and every run still ended off track at max_error about 0.0619 m, while progress fell (oval 0.42 to 0.31, s-bend 0.26 to 0.15). The off-track limit is max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4). At the widest allowed body (0.18 m) that is 0.0575 m, so the floor stays at 0.06 m and body width cannot help. The robot is now tracking-limited, not sensing-limited. Geometry can change how fast the robot can correct its heading. The turn rate is (vL - vR)/wheel_track, so for a given PWM difference a narrower track gives more yaw per command. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, so lower mass and a shorter body reduce the lag between a steering command and the heading change. Both changes should reduce the tracking lag that pushes max_error to 0.062 m. Changes: wheel_track 0.12 to 0.09 m, mass 0.8 to 0.6 kg, body_length 0.16 to 0.12 m. Sensor layout is kept exactly as in iteration 1 so the sensing result stays the same and any change comes from the drivetrain. Expected result: max_error below 0.06 on the oval and s-bend, some line-loss events still at 0, and the first completions possible. If max_error still sits at 0.062 with this agility, the limit is the controller gain or reaction point, not geometry.
